analysis.one_liner: Caps smog and soot pollution from power plants, with tradable allowances, penalties, and citizen lawsuits to enforce the caps.
analysis.headline: A bill to cut power-plant smog and soot — lowering the summer nitrogen-oxide cap in the 37-state eastern ozone region from 1.5 million tons in 1999 to 0.78 million tons by 2002 — died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote, despite 16 cosponsors split evenly between the parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set declining ceilings on total emissions of nitrogen oxides (the main ingredient of smog) and sulfur oxides (which form fine soot particles) from power plants across the eastern 37 states and the continental U.S. Plants would have received emission allowances they could trade, paid a $5,000-per-ton penalty for emitting more than their allowances, and faced citizen lawsuits for violations. It was written as electricity markets were being deregulated, to stop older, heavily polluting coal plants from undercutting cleaner competitors on price.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe air downwind of fossil-fueled power plants — especially in the 37 eastern states covered by the summer smog-season caps — would get lower exposure to nitrogen oxides and sulfate fine particles, pollutants the bill's own findings link to public health harm. Cleaner-burning plants, renewable generators, and companies that reduce electricity demand would benefit competitively: the bill ends the regulatory advantage old coal plants enjoyed and even awards emission allowances for verified energy conservation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents; cleaner power and conservation firms

how_it_helps.text: Sets statutory tonnage caps that tighten over time: summer nitrogen-oxide emissions in the 37-state OTAG region drop from 1.5 million tons (1999) to 1.0 million (2001) to 0.78 million tons (2002–2004), and national sulfur-oxide emissions fall from 4.45 million tons (2000–2004) to 4.0 million tons from 2005 onward.

Closes the loophole that let older generating units pollute at rates far above newer ones — the bill's findings note some old units emit nitrogen oxides approaching 10 times more per unit of electricity generated — which mattered because electricity deregulation was about to let those dirty plants undercut cleaner competitors on price.

Backs the caps with teeth: continuous emissions monitoring, a $5,000-per-ton penalty (indexed to inflation) for emissions above held allowances, a requirement to offset excess emissions later, and citizen suits against violators or against the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission if it fails to do its job.

Awards allowances to anyone who verifiably reduces electricity demand, so conservation gets paid the same way generation does, and requires the commission to publish its generation estimates and standards at least 30 days before each period so companies can plan.

analysis.who_pays: Owners of the covered fossil-fueled generating units — above all the operators of older coal-fired plants that had been running under looser rules — would bear the cost of cutting emissions, buying allowances, and paying $5,000 per excess ton. Some of that cost would likely reach electricity customers through rates, which is the tradeoff any emissions cap carries; the trading system is designed to keep the total cost lower by letting plants that can cut cheaply sell allowances to those that cannot.
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners of older fossil-fueled power plants

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for utilities would likely flow at least partly into electricity rates, a real cost to households that the trading system reduces but does not eliminate.

Allowance trading lets a plant keep polluting locally by buying credits earned elsewhere, so a specific community near a high-emitting plant could still face concentrated pollution even as regional totals fall; the bill's ozone-episode rule (multiplying reported emissions by up to 3 during smog episodes) only partially addresses this.

The bill hands an air-quality program to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, an agency set up to regulate electricity markets rather than public health, though it does allow the President to transfer the function to another agency if that would be more efficient.
Only units with 15 megawatts or more of capacity are covered, so smaller emitters escape the caps entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health side of the ledger is large: deep cuts in smog-forming and soot-forming emissions across the eastern half of the country, enforced by meaningful penalties and citizen suits, at a time when electricity deregulation would otherwise have rewarded the dirtiest plants. The costs — somewhat higher electricity prices for utilities and their customers, and the discomfort of placing environmental standard-setting with an economic regulator — are real but were the deliberate price of fitting pollution limits into a competitive market. The design (tradeable allowances, conservation credits, published standards) is a genuine attempt to lower the cost of the cuts. On balance, the benefits to residents of the affected region outweighed the costs; the bill's main flaw is that it never got the chance to be tested, amended, or debated.

outcome.mechanism: Two weeks after introduction it was sent to the House Commerce Committee's Energy and Power Subcommittee, which never held it, and it died there when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on November 7, 1997, joined by 15 original cosponsors — nearly the entire New Jersey House delegation from both parties, plus Rep. Henry Waxman of California.
The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and on November 20, 1997, sent along to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed. That was the bill's last recorded action for the remaining thirteen months of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of older, heavily polluting power plants came out ahead: they kept operating under their existing, looser limits and kept the competitive advantage over cleaner plants that the bill was written to remove, while residents of the 37-state ozone region did not get the promised emission cuts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of old, heavily polluting power plants

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to cap power-plant nitrogen oxide and sulfur emissions as electricity markets were restructured.

for.name: 16 House cosponsors (8 Republicans, 8 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in bipartisan support, drawn heavily from the New Jersey delegation, a state downwind of midwestern coal plants, plus Henry Waxman of California.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership (Chair Thomas Bliley)
against.role: Committee chair with authority to schedule the bill
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee; after the November 20, 1997 subcommittee referral, no further action of any kind was taken.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Power (Chair Joe Barton)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — 8 Republicans and 8 Democrats, mostly New Jerseyans — but it sat in a Republican-controlled committee and subcommittee that never moved it, and no vote was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Coal-fired electric utilities (especially owners of older plants)
industries.note: These plants were the bill's direct target: their exemption-style legacy rules let them emit nitrogen oxides at rates approaching 10 times newer units, an advantage the bill would have stripped and priced with $5,000-per-ton penalties. Their gain from the bill's death was the public's loss of cleaner air.

industries.industry: Cleaner fossil generators and renewable power producers
industries.note: By capping regional emissions and charging every covered unit the same per-megawatt-hour standard, the bill would have removed the cost advantage dirty plants held over plants that already run clean, rewarding investments those companies had already made.
The bill let anyone who verifiably reduced electricity demand earn emission allowances, converting conservation into a tradeable asset for the first time under the Federal Power Act.
